# Acta for coding agents

Describes Acta 1.0.0-rc.14: the packages Acta.Sqlite, Acta.Postgres, Acta.SqlServer, Acta.Dashboard, and
Acta.AspNetCore at that version. Verified 2026-11-17. When this file and an installed package disagree, the
package wins: the compiler and `<app> jobs help` outrank this file. In an existing app, read its resolved Acta
version first and follow the docs at that tag, github.com/acta-dotnet/acta/tree/v<version>; do not upgrade
the app to match an example. An upgrade made on purpose applies the "What a consumer must change" items of every
release between the two versions, in `docs/release-notes.md`.

Acta is a durable job and workflow engine for .NET backed by the application's own SQL database
(PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or embedded SQLite). One handler can record steps and variables, start
child jobs and fan out with Map and WaitChildren, and wait for signals and timers without
holding a worker; lanes keep per-entity order, and concurrency and rate limits hold across every
worker. Jobs, schedules, steps, waits, and alerts are ordinary rows. This file is the contract an agent needs to add Acta to a project correctly; the
runnable proof lives in the repository's `learn/` directory (compiled, one project per how-to) and the
complete demo apps under `demos/`. Start at useacta.net or github.com/acta-dotnet/acta.

## The one rule everything follows from

Execution is at-least-once, and a handler re-enters from the top. After a crash, a lease expiry, a
retry, or a resumed wait, Acta runs the handler method again from its first line. Completed steps,
variables, timers, and signal waits return their recorded results instead of repeating
their work; every bare line between them runs again on every entry. The model is checkpoints, not
deterministic replay: there is no determinism requirement on your code, and there is no magic resume-at-line-N.
Where these docs say a re-entry replays a step, the step answers from its record and its body does not run (the
`acta.steps` meter counts such a step under the outcome `reused`, and a step its check answered under `found`).
A crash counts against the retry budget: the attempt a dead worker held is reclaimed as a failed one, so
`MaxAttempts` crashes since the job last succeeded fail a job that never threw (a wait or a sleep is not a success,
so the count carries across them), and a reclaimed job is due again at once, without the backoff: it waits behind
work that was due before it and passes the same concurrency and rate gates as any claim.
The reclaim is `job.execution-orphaned` (reason `lease-expired`) on the timeline, or `job.failed` with that reason when
it spent the last attempt. With the default 45-second heartbeat a lost attempt comes back
three to about seven minutes after its worker's last heartbeat (one to two leases, plus up to a heartbeat for the
recovery pass). On SQLite, with crash recovery on (the default), a restart brings it back at once: a starting
worker releases its namespace's workers on the same machine whose process has ended, with their jobs' locks and
concurrency slots, and runs the recovery pass, whose reclaim of those jobs carries the reason `process-ended` (server databases wait out the lease, because replicas that share a
host name have process ids of their own). A clean stop is not a crash: running handlers finish first, up to the host's
`HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` (30 seconds by default), and only then is their token cancelled.

Those recorded results and the ledger make re-entry something you can reason about and test, because
everything a handler decided is a row you can read. Write handlers as if the method will be
called twice with the same input, and put every external side effect behind a step.

## First run: one file, one job, the dashboard

```bash
dotnet new web -n Shipping && cd Shipping
dotnet add package Acta.Sqlite --prerelease
dotnet add package Acta.Dashboard --prerelease
```

Replace `Program.cs` with this, all of it:

```csharp
using Shipping;                 // the generated manifest lands in your project's root namespace
using Acta;
using Acta.Dashboard;
using Acta.Sqlite;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.UseActa(j =>
{
    j.UseSqlite(sqlite =>
    {
        sqlite.ConnectionString = "Data Source=acta-local.db";
        sqlite.MigrateOnStartup = true;   // local development only; in production a deploy step runs "jobs migrate"
    });
    j.Run<ShippingJobs>("shipping");
});

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapActa("/acta");           // dashboard + JSON API; local-only by default, controls disabled

// Your own endpoint enqueues: the job is a durable row before the response goes out.
app.MapPost("/orders/{orderId:int}", async (int orderId, IJobs jobs) =>
{
    var job = await jobs.EnqueueAsync(new ShipOrder(orderId));
    return Results.Accepted("/acta", new { job.JobRef });
});

app.Run();

public sealed record ShipOrder(int OrderId);

public static class ShippingHandlers
{
    [Job("ship-order")]
    public static void Handle(ShipOrder input) => Console.WriteLine($"Shipping order {input.OrderId}");
}
```

`dotnet run`, then `curl -X POST http://localhost:<port>/orders/1042` on the port it printed: the app prints
`Shipping order 1042` and the dashboard lists the job. Rules this sample carries:

- `[Job("ship-order")]` is required and a name: dotted kebab-case, `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*` segments joined by `.`
  (`billing.send-invoice`), no underscores, no trailing dash, at most 128 chars. The bare `sys` and the `sys.` prefix are reserved for Acta's own jobs. The name is
  the durable operator-facing contract in SQL, the dashboard, the CLI, and alerts. The names you give steps, variables,
  signals, timers and children follow the same rule after folding to lowercase, so a per-item name puts a letter
  before the id: `apply-{orderId}` or `apply.o{orderId}`, never `apply/{orderId}`, and never `apply.{orderId}` when
  the id can start with a digit. An invalid one fails the job at once, since no retry can fix it, and the build
  refuses one it can already see is broken (ACTA0152). A raised signal value or a stored step result the code can no
  longer read fails the job at once too, naming the signal or step and the type.
- An attempt is cut off at its `ExecutionTimeout`, 5 minutes unless `[Job("import-catalog", ExecutionTimeout = "2h")]` says otherwise,
  and the cut spends an attempt. A long loop either sets it, or records each chunk as a step and yields every few
  minutes with `await ctx.RescheduleAsync(TimeSpan.Zero, ct: ct)`, which starts a fresh execution, its recorded
  chunks replayed, without spending budget.
- `ShippingJobs` is the source-generated manifest, named from the LAST segment of the project's
  `RootNamespace` plus `Jobs` (`Users` → `UsersJobs`; a segment already ending in `Jobs` gets
  `Manifest` instead: `TestJobs` → `TestJobsManifest`). It is generated into that root namespace,
  so a `Program.cs` of top-level statements, which sit in the global namespace, needs `using Shipping;` to see it.
- `"shipping"` in `j.Run<ShippingJobs>("shipping")` is the namespace, and it is permanent. It is the name the
  worker's jobs, schedules, idempotency keys, locks and rate meters are stored under, and the dashboard, the CLI,
  the HTTP API (`jobNamespace`) and SQL show it beside every job. There is no rename: jobs stored under an old name
  stay there with no worker to run them. Choose it once, for the work the app owns (`shipping`, `billing`), never
  for an environment, a version, a machine or a project's working title. It follows the name rule above, at most
  64 chars. Take it from what the app does, not from the folder name, and tell the user which name you chose and
  that it is permanent.
- Enqueue is type-driven: the input record's type routes the call, one `EnqueueAsync` for every
  job. It answers a `JobHandle`: `await job.WaitAsync()` follows the job without stopping it, for up to 30 seconds unless you pass a `TimeSpan`; branch on `TimedOut` before reading a result.
  `ScheduleAsync(input, TimeSpan)` or `ScheduleAsync(input, DateTimeOffset)` runs one job later; a recurring
  schedule is `[Schedule]`. The host that enqueues can also execute; there is no separate worker process
  unless you want one.
- A schedule's instants come from a cron, an interval, or a calendar bound by name (`Calendar = "pay-days"`),
  and any schedule fires only inside an availability calendar's windows when it names one
  (`Availability = "office-hours"`). A name is a catalog family, defined as JSON and published through
  `IActaOperations.Calendars`, the HTTP API, or the dashboard's Calendars page, in the namespace or shared in `sys`.
  Publish it before the deploy of the jobs that name it: a deploy whose schedule names a calendar with no
  published version fails and writes nothing. The page is `docs/scheduling.md`.
- Each job's member on `ShippingJobs` is named after the job in Pascal case (`ship-order` is `ShipOrder`,
  `permit.consultation` is `PermitConsultation`), a factory taking the handler's input parameters and returning the
  job's call: `jobs.EnqueueAsync(ShippingJobs.ShipOrder(new ShipOrder(orderId)))` names the job outright, and a
  result job's call answers `JobHandle<TResult>`. An enqueue that reads no result can pass the input alone, options
  included: `jobs.EnqueueAsync(new ShipOrder(orderId), o => o.IdempotencyKey(key))`. A handler may take several input parameters before `JobContext` and
  `CancellationToken`; they travel as one generated record, `ShippingJobs.{Job}Args`, whose parameter names
  are stored JSON keys. Under Native AOT, declare the input record yourself and take it as the one parameter: the build fails with ACTA0107 otherwise, and a host without reflection refuses to start when a job's JSON input or result type is missing from the context.
- The handle follows the job without another lookup: `await handle.WaitAsync()` answers its outcome, `await handle.GetResultAsync<ShipmentLabel>()` returns the stored result
  and throws when there is none, and `await handle.TryGetResultAsync<ShipmentLabel>()` answers `(Found, Value)` for a result that may not exist yet; on the `JobHandle<TResult>` a generated call answers, drop the type argument.
  From a ref the same reads are on `IJobs`: `jobs.GetResultAsync<ShipmentLabel>(jobRef)`. Neither read waits.
- An `IJobs` call that addresses a job takes a `JobLookup`, and both the handle an enqueue answered and a `JobRef` convert to one, so pass what you hold: `jobs.GetStatusAsync(jobRef)`. A ref that arrives as text, from a route or a column of your own, is `JobRef.Parse(text)` or `JobRef.TryParse`. `JobLookup.ByIdempotencyKey(jobNamespace, key)` finds the job a key made.
- Handlers resolve through DI: an instance class's constructor dependencies must be registered. One DI cannot build fails its job on the first attempt with `HandlerActivationException`, never retried, and the message names the missing service.

## Wiring rules by situation

- New app: ASP.NET Core empty host + `Acta.Sqlite` + `Acta.Dashboard` with `MapActa("/acta")` and
  one real job, exactly as above.
- Existing app: inspect its hosting and database first and preserve both. Add the matching
  provider package (`Acta.Postgres` / `Acta.SqlServer` / `Acta.Sqlite`) and register with the
  existing connection string; do not change the host type to add Acta.
- Producer and worker in the same assembly: typed `EnqueueAsync` plus `j.Run<TManifest>(...)`, as
  above. This is the default.
- A manifest is per assembly: every `[Job]` in a project lands in its one manifest, and `j.Run<TManifest>("ns")` registers
  them all in that namespace. Namespaces with different jobs take one project each. A namespace's expired leases are
  reclaimed by its own workers' recovery pass, so while it has no live worker its lost jobs stay `executing`.
- Split deployment (API enqueues, separate worker executes): the worker registers
  `Run<TManifest>`; the producer enqueues by the raw route contract instead of the typed call so
  it does not need the handler assembly.
- Never enable `MigrateOnStartup` outside an explicitly local or development configuration. There, startup applies the schema and writes the app's jobs and schedules, so one `dotnet run` is enough. An app that owns its SQLite file, such as a desktop tool or a single-file exe, is such a local configuration.
- Production runs `<app> jobs migrate` from a deploy step before the new build starts: it applies the schema, deploys the app's job definitions and schedules, and records the app's version. `<app> jobs deploy` does the deploy alone and needs no DDL right. A worker start writes no definition or schedule, and refuses a namespace its build's version has not deployed in.
- Once `jobs migrate` or `jobs deploy` has deployed a namespace, a `MigrateOnStartup` start writes no definition or schedule there, on a local database too: a new or changed job then takes `jobs deploy`, or a fresh local database.
- Give each build its own version: `JobsOptions.DeploymentVersion`, by default the entry assembly's informational version. An app that is `1.0.0` on every build is one version to Acta.
- A job that must exist only if your own write commits takes your transaction first: `await jobs.EnqueueAsync(transaction, new ShipOrder(orderId), ct: ct)` inserts it through your open `DbTransaction` (every enqueue shape has the overload), so the order row and its job commit or roll back together. It answers an `EnqueueJobResponse` (`JobRef`, `Action`), not a `JobHandle`, since the row exists only once you commit: follow the job after the commit with `jobs.WaitAsync(response.JobRef)`. A plain connection of your own needs nothing registered: Acta prepares a SQLite connection it is handed itself. Your tables may share Acta's database, a SQLite file included; Acta's tables are in its own schema, `acta` by default, which SQLite, having no schemas, puts before each name as a prefix (`acta_jobs`, `acta_steps`, `acta_events`, ...). Acta never commits or rolls back your transaction, and the job is picked up after the commit by polling, not at once. On SQLite keep it short: it holds the database's one write lock, which every Acta write in the process waits on. When the business data lives in another database, stage the job in an outbox table instead: `docs/developer-guide.md`, "Transactional enqueue and the external outbox".
- An external outbox table comes from the producer's own migrations (`CreateOutboxScript()`) or `ApplyOutboxAsync`; Acta never creates it on its own.
- On SQLite every Acta write in the process queues behind one in-process write queue and then waits for the file's write lock as long as the connection string's `Default Timeout` (30 s unless set; `CommandTimeout` does not bound that wait), and a write still refused is tried again, up to `DeadlockRetryAttempts` attempts in all (5 by default, the first included). A lock held shorter than that is a silent stall, not a failure; past it the caller sees the provider's own exception, `SqliteException` ("database is locked"), which an endpoint maps to 503. `acta.jobs.inflight` (by state: claimed, executing, finalizing) and `acta.completions.unsettled` on the `Acta` meter show what the process holds meanwhile. SQLite is built for one host process; several on one machine share the file correctly but are discouraged, since they take turns at that lock and an enqueue wakes only its own process. Hosts on several machines take PostgreSQL or SQL Server.
- Rolling deploys are routine: run `<app> jobs migrate`, start the new build, stop the old one, with any overlap. Acta's migrations are forward-only and keep an old and a new build working on one schema; a worker hands back a job whose handler it lacks and stops claiming that definition; a deploy never retires a definition the new build omits, so a rollback keeps the queue. What the application keeps is its own, as in any rolling deploy: a queued input the new build still reads, and a step name a running job still finds. Retiring a dropped definition and cancelling its queue is an operator action on the definition.
- Definitions and schedules are the current deployment's. An older build's workers write nothing, and its `jobs deploy` changes nothing unless run with `--force`, which is how a rollback restores the earlier definitions. A schedule a deploy drops is orphaned and loses its pause, so to hold a permanent job across a rollback, pause the job, not the schedule.

## Steps

`await ctx.RunStepAsync("name", ct => ...)` is a named run-once step. On re-entry a completed step
returns its recorded result instead of running the body. That promise has two conditions:

- The outcome is durable only after it is recorded. A crash after the side effect ran but before
  the outcome landed re-runs the body on replay, so the body must be idempotent, usually via a
  stable key derived from the job, never from the attempt. Where the provider can be asked, give the step a check:
  `ctx.RunStepWithCheckAsync(name, body, check)` asks it only when the step was started and never recorded, records
  a value it finds as the result without running the body, and runs the body on `null` (`false` for a step with no
  result). One outside effect per step, no wait inside the body (it fails the job at once), a lookup keyed to this
  job's own effect. It is not exactly-once.
- Only step-wrapped work is skipped. Bare handler code between steps re-runs on every entry.

A step retries through its job: a body that throws fails the attempt, the job's `MaxAttempts` and
`Backoff` retry it (by default 15 attempts, backing off from a minute to a day, about 4.4 days in all), and
the retry replays the steps that succeeded and runs this one again. A wait
inside a step body works: the resume runs the body up to the wait, which returns what it has, and
charges nothing. A step with a result returns a value: a body that returns null is recorded with no
result, and a replay answers null without running it again; a result past `MaxInlinePayloadBytes` is
stored with a warning, up to 16 MiB; a step with nothing to return takes a body that returns no value.

Every exception Acta has no reason to call final is retried, an `ArgumentException` or a validation
error included. Declare the types that can never succeed once, in `UseActa`:
`j.DoNotRetry<ArgumentException>();`. That type and every type derived from it then fails a job at
once, with no retry and no failure charged (reason `non-retryable-exception`); a permanent job's
firing fails and the job returns to Idle. Only the thrown exception is matched, never one it wraps. `ctx.FailAsync("why")` ends one job from inside its handler.

To compensate before a failure ends the job, catch on `ctx.EndsJob(ex)`:
`catch (Exception ex) when (ctx.EndsJob(ex)) { await ctx.RunStepAsync("release-stock", ...); throw; }`.
It is true for `ctx.FailAsync` and `CancelAsync`, for a non-retryable exception such as `StepFailedException` or a waited child's failure rethrown,
and for any other error on the last attempt (`ctx.IsLastAttempt` reads the budget the job has already
spent, and a Strict deadline, never the execution number); it is false for a wait, sleep, reschedule or
pause, which end only the attempt. That is best effort: a crash or a lost lease on the last attempt skips
the catch, so the compensation is an idempotent step, and work whose compensation must happen runs as a
child job the parent compensates when the child lands `Failed`.

Five handler calls end the attempt where they stand, by throwing: `ctx.FailAsync` and `ctx.CancelAsync` end the
job (`Failed`, `Cancelled`), `ctx.PauseAsync` holds it until a resume, and `ctx.RescheduleAsync` and
`ctx.RescheduleUntilAsync` run it again later. Nothing after one of them runs in that attempt, so an `if` that
ends in one needs no `else` and no `return`; only a handler that returns a value still owes the compiler a
`return` or a `throw` after it. After a pause or a reschedule the handler re-enters from its first line. A wait
or a sleep ends the attempt the same way the first time and answers from its record on the re-entry, so the
lines after it do run, in a later execution.

For side effects where a duplicate is worse than an ambiguous interruption (a payment capture),
`AtMostOnce()` runs the body zero-or-one times and hands the handler an explicit interrupted state to
reconcile. A body that throws fails the step for good: every later attempt throws `StepFailedException`
for it without running the body, so left uncaught it fails the job at once; catch it where the job can
go on, and an operator restart runs the step again. A body that cannot know the outcome, a timeout after
the request left, throws `OutcomeUnknownException` instead: the step ends as a crash ends it, the call throws
`StepInterruptedException`, and no retry or restart runs the body again
(`catch (TimeoutException ex) { throw new OutcomeUnknownException("capture timed out", ex); }`). A wait inside an
at-most-once body throws at the call, because its resume would run the body again; inside the body of a step
with a check it throws too, because the resume would ask the check and skip the rest of the body.

## An external side effect, done right

```csharp
using Acta;

namespace Shipping;

public sealed record DeliverWebhook(Guid DeliveryId, string Url, string Payload);

// The receiver refused the payload itself, so no retry can change its answer.
public sealed class WebhookRejected(int status) : Exception($"The receiver refused the webhook with {status}.");

public sealed class WebhookJobs(HttpClient http)
{
    [Job("deliver-webhook", MaxAttempts = 5)]
    public async Task Handle(DeliverWebhook input, JobContext ctx, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        try
        {
            await ctx.RunStepAsync("post", async token =>
            {
                using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, input.Url);
                // The receiver's idempotency key comes from the JOB (stable across attempts), never the attempt.
                request.Headers.Add("Idempotency-Key", input.DeliveryId.ToString());
                request.Content = new StringContent(input.Payload);
                using var response = await http.SendAsync(request, token);
                if ((int)response.StatusCode is >= 400 and < 500 and not 408 and not 429)
                {
                    throw new WebhookRejected((int)response.StatusCode);
                }
                response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode(); // a 5xx, a 408 or a 429 throws, and the attempt retries
            }, ct);
        }
        catch (WebhookRejected rejected)
        {
            await ctx.FailAsync(rejected.Message, ct); // ends the job now: a retry would get the same answer
        }
    }
}
```

Register `HttpClient` in DI (`builder.Services.AddHttpClient<WebhookJobs>();`). A step that recorded
its outcome is reused on re-entry, so a crash after `post` recorded never sends again. The window for a
duplicate is narrower: the receiver accepted the request, then the process died before Acta recorded
the `post` outcome. The retry sends again with the same `Idempotency-Key`, because the key comes from
the job's input and not from the attempt, and the receiver deduplicates on it. That is the
at-least-once contract working: an effect can repeat only under its own key. Which answers retry is
the application's call: throw for them inside the step, and end the job with `FailAsync` outside it for
an answer no retry changes. Never return the refusal as the step's result and fail after it: the step
would record success with the refusal in it, and a restart would never send again.

## Do this, not that

| Instead of | Do | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| static/instance fields for progress | `SetVariableAsync` / `GetVariableOrDefaultAsync` | fields die with the process; variables are rows |
| computing a value fixed once (a quote, a snapshot) in a bare line | `await ctx.GetOrSetVariableAsync("quote", ct => ..., ct)` after the step that produced it, with a factory that returns a value: null stores nothing | the first stored value stays; a bare line recomputes on every re-entry |
| `Task.Delay` or `Thread.Sleep` | `await ctx.SleepAsync("cool-down", delay, ct: ct)` | delays hold a worker; durable sleep frees it and survives deploys |
| calling an API directly in the body | `await ctx.RunStepAsync("charge", ct => ...)` | a step records its outcome, so a retry does not repeat recorded work |
| `catch { }` around the body | let it throw, or `await ctx.FailAsync(reason)` | swallowing turns a retryable failure into a silent success |
| `catch (Exception)` around a wait, sleep or ctx call | `catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not JobControlException)`, or `when (ctx.EndsJob(ex))` to compensate | the call ends the attempt by throwing a `JobControlException` (a `finally` still runs); a handler that swallows it and returns fails at once, and `ACTA0151` warns at build time |
| polling a flag in a loop | `var r = await ctx.WaitSignalAsync("approved", timeout, ct)` | polling burns a worker; a signal parks the job, and the timeout keeps it from parking forever |
| enqueuing children and looping until they are done | `await ctx.WaitChildrenAsync([audit, receipt], ct)` on the children you enqueued (a `TimeSpan` before the token sets a deadline), or `MapAsync` when the children come from a list | the parent parks instead of occupying a worker |
| `jobs.CallAsync` or `handle.WaitAsync()` on an injected `IJobs` inside a handler | `await ctx.CallChildAsync("label", ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(input), ct)` (in these samples `print-label` returns a `ShipmentLabel`; in `docs/first-job.md` it returns nothing), or `EnqueueChildAsync` and a wait later | an `IJobs` wait holds the worker until the job ends or the wait times out, and each re-entry enqueues another job; a child call parks the job, and its name finds the same child |
| `Task.WhenAll` over several `CallChildAsync` calls | `EnqueueChildAsync` each, then one `await ctx.WaitChildrenAsync([email, sms], ct)` | the group wait wakes the parent only when the child it waits on lands, where `Task.WhenAll` wakes it on every landing, and a timeout on it is one deadline for every child |
| `DateTime.Now` | `DateTime.UtcNow`, or a value from the input | the ledger is UTC throughout |

## Waiting for an outside event

A handler parks on a named signal and something outside raises it: a webhook, an operator, another
job. `await ctx.WaitSignalAsync("shipped", ct)` parks until the raise, and
`await ctx.WaitSignalAsync<Shipped>("shipped", ct)` returns the raised value, null when the signal was
raised without one. A wait that can time out answers an outcome instead:
`var r = await ctx.WaitSignalAsync<Shipped>("shipped", TimeSpan.FromDays(14), ct);` returns a
`SignalWaitOutcome<T>`, so branch on `r.TimedOut` and read `r.Value`, or call `r.ValueOrThrow()`
(or `r.ThrowIfTimedOut()`, on either outcome) to fail the job at once when the deadline passed; it answers null for a raise that
carried no value, and `r.HasValue`, like `r.TryGetValue(out var shipped)`, is true only for a raise that carried one. An outcome left
unread lets the handler carry on past the deadline. The raising side is
`await jobs.RaiseSignalAsync(jobRef, "shipped", new Shipped(trackingId), ct)` on `IJobs`, and an
`actor:` argument before the token names who raised it. It answers an `Action` (a `ControlAction`) and the job's `Status` after the call,
so a job parked on the wait reads `Ready`: the raise re-armed it. `Applied` means stored, not taken: a name no wait
ever asks for is `Applied` too, so a raise authenticates and correlates nothing; check the caller first. An unknown
job answers `NotFound`. A raise commits on its own, never in your transaction,
so a crash between your commit and the raise leaves the wait to time out: let the timeout branch re-read your own
record. A raise that comes before the handler reaches its wait
is stored, and the wait reads it without parking. The deadline is stored once, as
database time plus the timeout, so restarts and downtime never lengthen it; on SQLite, database time is SQLite's
clock, which can trail `DateTime.UtcNow` by a clock tick (about 16 ms on Windows). A raise wins until the parked
job re-enters, even after the deadline has passed: the job wakes at its deadline, and only its re-entry settles
the wait expired. A wait's timeout rounds up to whole seconds, at least one, so a wait whose span is zero or less
still parks about a second before it times out (a sleep of zero or less returns at once). A deadline shared by
several waits is an instant: `await ctx.WaitSignalAsync("approval", deadline, ct)` takes a `DateTimeOffset` and
stores it as the wait's expiration, and a wait first armed at or past it times out at once. The expiry writes `job.wait-expired` naming the signal or child and its deadline. An expired wait stays expired, and a late raise answers
`Rejected` with `Reason` `wait-expired`. Only a restart reopens one: the timed-out wait that ended the job. A wait bounded by a
timeout then waits again under a fresh bound, and one bounded by an instant meets that instant again and times out at once; a
timeout the handler went past stays as it was.
A signal keeps the value of its first raise: raising it again with the same value answers `AlreadyInState`, after
the job finished too, and with another value `Rejected` (`Reason` `value-differs`), so a wait that already returned never reads a different value on replay. A raise on a finished job answers `Rejected` with `job-finished`; the reason is in the HTTP 409 body and the CLI's output too.
The values compare as stored bytes, so keep volatile fields (a timestamp, a per-attempt id) out of a raised value: a
retry after a lost answer then repeats the same value and answers `AlreadyInState`.
A second window, or a second value, is a wait under a new name (`"shipped-2"`) or a new job.
A finished job, or a permanent job between firings, forgets a signal with `jobs.ClearSignalAsync(job, name)`
(`DELETE /jobs/{jobRef}/signals/{name}`, which has no JSON body and so sends the header `X-Acta-Control: true`;
`<app> jobs clear-signal <job> <name>`), recorded as `job.signal-cleared`
with the actor. To give a finished job's signal another value, clear it, restart the job, then raise it. A live job
keeps its signals: the clear answers `Rejected` with `Reason` `job-not-finished` (`system-job` for a `sys.` job),
and a name with no signal `AlreadyInState`.

## Child jobs and fan-out

A handler sends other jobs as children and parks until they end. The parent holds no worker while it
waits, and each child is an ordinary job with its own row, retries, and steps. The first argument of
every call is a name, and the name makes the send run-once: on re-entry the same name finds the child
it already enqueued.

One rule names every call: a handler's call is the `IJobs` call with `Child` after its first verb.

- *Enqueue* sends a job without waiting: `jobs.EnqueueAsync`, `ctx.EnqueueChildAsync`.
- *Call* sends a job and waits for its outcome: `jobs.CallAsync`, `ctx.CallChildAsync`.
- *Wait* follows a job sent earlier: `jobs.WaitAsync`, `ctx.WaitChildAsync`, and `ctx.WaitChildrenAsync` for several.
- A result is read with `jobs.GetResultAsync<T>` or `ctx.GetChildResultAsync<T>`.

*Run* is work the handler does itself (`RunStepAsync`), never a child. An `IJobs` wait holds its caller
until the job ends or the wait times out; a handler's wait parks the job and holds no worker.

| To | Call | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| call one child | `await ctx.CallChildAsync("email", new SendEmail(orderId), ct)` | `JobOutcome`: `Succeeded`, `Status`, `ThrowIfFailed()` |
| call one child and read its result | `await ctx.CallChildAsync("label", ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(new PrintLabel(orderId)), ct)` | `JobOutcome<TResult>`: also `Value`, `HasValue`, `TryGetValue`, `ValueOrThrow()` |
| call one child per item of a list | `await ctx.MapAsync("reserve", skus, itemKey: sku => sku, child: sku => new ReserveStock(orderId, sku), ct)` | `MapOutcome<TKey>`: `Items` (each `Key` and `Outcome`), `Failed`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` |
| read a result per item of a list | `await ctx.MapAsync("label", orders, o => o.Id, o => ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(new PrintLabel(o.Id)), ct)` | `MapOutcome<TKey, TResult>`: each item's `Outcome.ValueOrThrow()` |
| call different jobs at once, or enqueue now and wait later | `var email = await ctx.EnqueueChildAsync("email", new SendEmail(orderId), ct);` and `sms` alike, then `await ctx.WaitChildrenAsync([email, sms], ct)` | `ChildrenWaitOutcome`: `Children`, `Succeeded`, `Failed`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` |

- A failed or cancelled child never throws in the parent by itself. Every wait answers an outcome and the handler decides: `ThrowIfFailed()` or `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` to fail with it, or branch on `Failed` and compensate. A group waits for every child; it never fails fast and never cancels siblings.
- Every child ends in a `JobOutcome`, alone or as a member of a group: `JobRef`, `Status`, `Succeeded`, `TimedOut`, and `ThrowIfFailed()`. A child that failed carries the message it failed with in `FailureMessage`, and `ThrowIfFailed()` puts it in the parent's failure; one that crash recovery failed carries none. `IJobs.WaitAsync` answers the same type outside a handler, with no `FailureMessage`: read that job's timeline. Wait now with `CallChildAsync`; wait later for children you enqueued, one or many, with `WaitChildrenAsync`; fan a list out with `MapAsync`.
- `ThrowIfFailed()`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` and `ValueOrThrow()` in a handler fail the job at once, with no retry: a retry would find the same failed child. To recover, restart the child, then the parent: restarting a child puts its parent's wait for it back to pending, so the parent waits for the child's new outcome whether it runs before or after the child lands. A bounded wait keeps its deadline: a child restarted after that deadline has passed is timed out and cancelled when the parent next runs. A parent restarted alone reads the same failed child and fails again at once. A restarted parent keeps the results of the steps after its wait, so bind a decision you derive from the children's outcomes into the step that acts on it.
- A child's name is its `IdempotencyKey` on the job reads: the call's name for `CallChildAsync` and `EnqueueChildAsync`, and `{map}/{key}` for a map's child (`sections/coast`; a key that is not lowercase letters, digits and single dashes becomes a hash, so lowercase a key you want to read in the name), so `acta.Ledger.ListJobsAsync(new ListJobsQuery(Parent: parent.JobRef))` lists the children by name. A name is unique only under its parent, so `JobLookup.ByIdempotencyKey` finds root jobs only, never a child.
- A child alerts on its own failure as its definition's `AlertProfile` says (`OnFailure` by default), also when the
  parent expects the failure and compensates for it. When the parent reports it, declare the child
  `[Job("reserve-room", AlertProfile = AlertProfileCode.None)]`; an alert the parent raises is still created.
- A child's result rides on the outcome when the child is the manifest's call (`ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(...)`), alone with `CallChildAsync` or per item with `MapAsync`. For a child you enqueued and waited for, read it by id: `await ctx.GetChildResultAsync<string>(child.JobId, ct)` throws when there is none, and `TryGetChildResultAsync<T>` answers `(Found, Value)`.
- `MapAsync` and `WaitChildrenAsync` take a `TimeSpan` timeout before the token: one deadline for the whole group, which cancels only the members still running and reports `TimedOut` on the outcome. `MapAsync` takes one `configure` that every child gets. A replay starts only the children not yet started, without running the `child` selector or `configure` for one already started.
- A generated call passed where an input is expected, a map's child included, is enqueued by the job it names.
- A group does not limit how many of its children run at once; that is `ConcurrencyLimit` on the child's definition.
- The runnable proof is `learn/200-durable-execution/215-map-wait-children`; a failed child's outcomes are in `219-child-failure-outcomes`.

## Recurring work

`[Schedule("every-5s", "PT5S")]` on a `[Job]` makes a permanent job: one durable job the schedule
fires again and again. A schedule faster than once a minute makes the build warn (ACTA0108) until the
job states `EventRecording`, for example `EventRecording = EventRecordingCode.Failures`. The job sits `Idle` between firings and holds no thread; the admission
engine makes it `Ready` when a schedule is due, a worker claims it like any job, and the handler
returns when its bounded work is done. Never loop forever inside the handler and never poll from it:
a firing that finds nothing to do returns, and the next firing comes on schedule. Acta's progress is
the schedule cursor (`next_occurrence_at_utc`); the handler's progress, such as a synchronization
watermark, is a durable variable on the job (`ctx.GetVariableOrDefaultAsync` at the top of every
execution, `ctx.SetVariableAsync` after the work it covers), carried across firings, retries, and
workers, so a recovered firing continues where the lost one stopped. Write the work first and the
variable after it, and make the work an upsert: an attempt that dies between the two replays one
batch. A definition whose occurrences are each their own job, with
their own retries, result, and retention, declares `ScheduledDelivery = ScheduledDeliveryCode.PerOccurrence`.
A finite schedule declares `StartAtUtc` and `EndBeforeUtc` (UTC with a `Z`): its occurrences fall in
[start, end) and it reads `exhausted` past the end. The runnable proof, with a killed worker, is
`learn/100-scheduling/109-continuous-synchronization`.

## Choosing between a lane, a key, a limit, and a rate

One axis each: a lane decides ORDER, a concurrency key and its limit decide HOW MANY run at once, and a
rate decides HOW OFTEN. For one job at a time per customer, account, or aggregate, use a lane: it adds
order, and the jobs waiting behind its head cost the claim nothing, where a busy key's waiting jobs are
claimed, bounced, and re-armed. Use a bare `ConcurrencyKey` only when order must not hold work up: a
lane's failing head blocks the jobs behind it until it succeeds or exhausts MaxAttempts, and a key's
does not. Use `ConcurrencyLimit` for N at once and `RateLimit` for pacing; they combine. A limit's slot
is held while an attempt runs, not while the job sleeps or waits, so a resource a job holds for its
whole life, a machine or a room, is a lane: the next job behind it starts only when this one ends.

## Limiting how much runs at once

`options.ConcurrencyKey("rebuild:acme")` on an enqueue admits one job of that key at a time,
cluster-wide: the runner takes the key's lease after the claim and before the handler, and a loser
re-arms Ready a couple of seconds out without spending retry budget. `[Job("rebuild-index",
ConcurrencyLimit = 4)]` sizes that gate: the key gets four concurrency slots instead of one. When an enqueue
supplies no key, the definition name is the key, so a limit alone throttles the whole definition. Two
definitions on the same key share its slots and the key's capacity is the largest limit among them.
It is mutual exclusion, never ordering: an older job can be overtaken while the key stays busy.
Each bounce is an execution of its own (the job's `ExecutionNumber` moves and the timeline gains its rows), so a
long queue behind a narrow key writes many rows; a lane, which holds its queue `Blocked` and claims only the head,
writes none for waiting. A slot held by a worker that died frees when that worker's lease lapses; recovery reclaims the job after that.
For one section of a handler rather than the whole job, `await ctx.RunWithLockAsync("ledger:acme", ct => ..., ct: ct)`
runs the action under a lock on an opaque key, scoped to the namespace; acquiring waits about 30 seconds (the
`timeout:` argument) before it throws `LockAcquisitionTimeoutException`. The hold renews with the holder's
heartbeat, so a dead holder keeps the key for up to one lease, the same window as its job's lease.

## Running jobs in order

`options.Lane("customer-42")` on an enqueue, or `[Job("sync-orders", Lane = "orders")]` on a
definition, puts the job in a lane: one job of the lane runs at a time, in enqueue order, like an SQS
FIFO message group. The jobs behind the head are `Blocked` until it finishes (Succeeded, Failed on
its last attempt, or Cancelled), and a failing head keeps retrying in place, holding the lane. A paused head holds
it until resumed, and a head whose worker died holds it until recovery reclaims it: three to about seven
minutes at the default heartbeat. `Blocked` says
only that a job is behind the head, whatever the head is doing (running, retrying, or waiting for a person), so
a screen that tells a hold from a queue reads the head: the lane's one unfinished job that is not `Blocked`. A lane
is order, not a condition: the next job runs after a failed or cancelled head too, so a job that may
only follow a success checks for it in its first step. Rows
staged in sequence through the outbox with a lane reach it in staging order, a rejected row keeping its place. An
enqueue lane overrides the definition's. A lane is a name: ASCII dotted kebab-case up to 128 characters,
lowercased on input. Rules that bite: never enqueue a child into the lane of an unfinished ancestor (refused
at enqueue), never put a lane on a scheduled definition (refused), give waits across lanes a timeout,
and restart of a finished laned job runs that job again, right after the lane's current head.

`[Job("send-invoice", RateLimit = "10/s")]` paces how OFTEN attempts are admitted, which is a
different gate from how many run at once, and a job passes both. It takes the concurrency slot first and then the
rate turn, and one the meter books for later gives its slot back, so with a rate and a narrow key on one job most of
a backlog bounces off the key before the meter books it. The value is a count per second,
minute, or hour, `N/s`, `N/m`, or `N/h`, at most 1000 a second: one every four seconds is `15/m`.
It paces admissions, not starts,
and is no hard burst cap: a turn admitted late can land beside an on-time one. Every execution takes a
turn, a retry and a resume after a wait included, so a handler that waits meets its own meter on each
re-entry: to pace one outside call inside a longer workflow, put the rate on a small child job that
makes the call. `RateName` names
the meter when several definitions should share one; omitted, the meter is the definition name.
A meter belongs to one namespace: definitions in different namespaces never share it, so a partner
quota shared by two services needs its rate split between them. Definitions on one meter must
declare the same rate. A job that arrives early is BOOKED the next free instant: under a quarter second away
the executor sleeps it out and takes it, farther away the job re-arms Ready at exactly that instant
without spending retry budget (reason `rate-limited`, never a failure and never an alert). A booked
turn stays valid for a second, or for the rate's interval when that is longer, so a backlog drains
in arrival order at the rate with one re-arm per job; a job picked up later than that is metered
again.

## Tenants

- A tenant names who a job is about, a customer such as `acme-corp`; the namespace names who runs it. Register one
  with `await acta.Tenants.RegisterAsync("acme-corp", ct: ct)`, enqueue with `o => o.TenantName("acme-corp")`, and the
  handler reads `ctx.TenantName`. A child inherits its parent's tenant; naming another takes `overrideParent: true`.
- `[Job("bill-tenant", TenantRequirement = TenantRequirementCode.Required)]` refuses an enqueue without a tenant, and
  `Forbidden` one with a tenant.
- An unknown or suspended tenant's enqueue is refused (`EnqueueRejectionReason.TenantUnknown`, `TenantSuspended`).
  Suspension only stops admission: admitted jobs run on, the children they start are admitted, and restarts and
  signals still apply.
- An idempotency key is the namespace's, not the tenant's: an enqueue whose key another tenant's job holds is refused
  (`EnqueueRejectionReason.TenantMismatch`), naming neither the job nor the tenant, while a side with no tenant still
  matches. Build a tenant's key with `IdempotencyKey.ForTenant(tenantName, businessKey)`.
- A tenant is not a security boundary. Acta authorizes no caller by tenant: its reads filter by tenant only when asked,
  and its HTTP API and dashboard show every tenant to whoever holds the permission, so a tenant-facing app checks
  `TenantName` itself before it shows or controls a job.

## Payloads

What a caller sends inline (inputs, variables, signal values) is capped at 1 MiB (`MaxInlinePayloadBytes`).
Caller-supplied oversized writes throw `PayloadTooLargeException`. A handler or step RESULT past the
cap is stored, since the work behind it is already done, and the worker logs a warning; past 16 MiB, or past the cap
where a host set it higher, it fails the job for good. Big artifacts belong in blob storage with the
job carrying a reference: URI, checksum, size.

By default an input with no data uses the `none` format, `byte[]`/`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` use `bytes`, and every
other input, scalars included, is JSON (`"hello"`, `42`); an explicit or custom format overrides that. A raw or
HTTP enqueue in the json format sends strict JSON (one value, no comments or trailing commas) or is refused.
A JSON value binds leniently, as System.Text.Json does: a member it leaves out reads as its default, so a signal
raised as `{"note":"ok"}` reads an enum `Verdict` as its first value. Mark a member `required` when leaving it out
must be refused, and give an enum a first value that grants nothing (`Unset`).

## Things that are not what they sound like

- A `Suspended` job is healthy, not stuck: it is waiting on a signal or a child (a sleeping job reads `ready` with a future `NextRunAtUtc`). A wait
  armed with a timeout resolves itself when the deadline passes; an unbounded wait parks until
  raised.
- A wait, a sleep, a reschedule and a pause are exceptions: each ends the attempt by throwing a
  `JobControlException`, which the worker turns into the job's next state, so an attached debugger
  does not stop on them; it stops on errors. Every exception Acta defines derives from `ActaException`.
- An alert for a failed job is not instant. The `sys.alerts` job turns failure events into alerts once
  a minute, so one appears up to about two minutes after the failure. A handler that wants one now
  writes it: `await ctx.AlertAsync("Stock low", "Bin 7 is empty", AlertSeverityCode.Warning, ct: ct)`.
  An alert raised that way stays open until something resolves it: `AlertAsync` answers its `AlertRef`, and
  `acta.Alerts.ResolveAsync(alertRef)` resolves it from the step that fixed the cause (keep the ref in a variable
  across waits). One raised with a
  `deduplicationKey` resolves by that key from any job of its namespace, the job that opened it or another:
  `await ctx.ResolveAlertAsync("stock-low-bin-7", ct)` answers true when it resolved an open one, and
  `ctx.ResolveAlertAsync("stock-low-bin-7", "restocked by Sara", ct)` puts the reason on its `alert.resolved` event. The row is written at once; its delivery to
  the alert channel runs on the `sys.alerts` pass, so it reaches a channel within about a minute. The line runs again on every
  re-entry, like any bare line: without a `deduplicationKey` each run inserts another alert, and with one a
  repeat folds into the open alert, counting an occurrence, while a repeat after it was resolved opens a new one.
  To raise it once, raise it in a step: `await ctx.RunStepAsync("ring-engineer", _ => ctx.AlertAsync(...), ct)`.
- `acta.Definitions.UpdateOverridesAsync` replaces the definition's whole override set, and a null field clears
  that override: read `Overrides` from `GetAsync`, change it with `with { ConcurrencyLimit = 4 }`, and send it back
  with the definition's `version`. Workers take the change on their next heartbeat (`HeartbeatInterval`, 45
  seconds by default).
- Acta keeps finished work and its history for a year; change it in one place, and a job that should go
  sooner or stay longer says so. Retention deletes finished work only. A job that landed `Succeeded`,
  `Failed`, or `Cancelled` is deleted with its steps and checkpoints once its definition's retention has
  passed: `JobsOptions.Retention`, a year by default, which a deploy writes to every definition that states
  none, or the job's own (`[Job("send-digest", JobRetention = "7d")]`; `"never"` keeps it 2,147,483,647
  seconds, about 68 years). A job that waits is never deleted,
  however long it waits, and a finished child stays until its parent has finished and the parent's own retention is due. Events go by age,
  kept for `JobsOptions.Retention` too: a job still waiting after that keeps
  everything it needs to resume and loses the oldest lines of its timeline. Jobs and events both wait
  for the namespace's alert projector (`sys.alerts`) to read past them, so a stuck projector delays
  their deletion. A record the business must keep for good belongs in the application's own table,
  written in a step.
- Idempotency keys keep their case (printable ASCII, no whitespace, surrounding whitespace
  trimmed): `Order-1` and `order-1` are two keys, so lowercase an id yourself when its source is
  case-insensitive.
- The enqueue `idempotencyKey` prevents a second job ROW, not a second side effect; execution
  stays at-least-once either way. The handle tells which: `handle.Action` is `EnqueueJobAction.Deduplicated` when
  the key matched a job already there, `Inserted` when the enqueue created it. A key holds for as long as
  the job that has it exists, finished or not; retention frees it.
- An updated input does not recompute what already ran: a restart keeps every succeeded step, so those
  steps return what they computed from the old input. To recompute, enqueue a new job under a new
  idempotency key (`invoice-77.r2`) with the old job's correlation key; its steps and children start
  fresh, since a child's name is unique only within its parent.
- Tags are for finding jobs, not for carrying data: input is typed and versioned, tags are
  searchable labels.
- A permanent job keeps its step results, variables and signals from one fire to the next: a step
  that succeeded on Monday returns Monday's result on Tuesday, and Monday's signal answers Tuesday's
  wait. Put the period in the step or signal name (`$"invoice-{period}"`), or call `ctx.ResetStateAsync` as the handler's last action so the next fire
  starts clean. Never at the top: a reset there also runs on every retry and replay of the same fire,
  erasing its own progress, so succeeded steps run again and an `AtMostOnce` body can run twice. The reset clears
  variables too, so a watermark carried across fires is written after it, as the last line. A fire that fails for
  good never reaches its reset and leaves its steps to the next one, so name a fire's steps by the fire:
  `$"plan.f{ctx.FiringId:N}"`, since a GUID's hex can start with a digit and a name segment cannot.
- Children a permanent job starts are never purged while its schedule lives, since retention keeps a
  child as long as its parent. For per-occurrence fan-out, declare the definition
  `ScheduledDelivery = ScheduledDeliveryCode.PerOccurrence`: each occurrence is then a root job of its
  own, and the children it starts drain with it.

## Watch a job

Every Acta host is also a control CLI: `<app> jobs <verb>` runs against the app's own configured database
and exits, starting no worker, so it must run with the same configuration and environment as the app. The
argument `jobs` is reserved for it: a host started with `jobs` as its first argument, or its first after host
switches such as `--environment Staging`, runs the verb as the host starts and exits, so an app's own launcher never
passes `jobs` there. Code before `app.Run` still runs on that path; guard host-only startup work (seeding, your own
files) with `if (!args.Contains("jobs"))`.
Keep the job ref an enqueue returns (`job_...`); it is the job's public identity everywhere.

```bash
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs status  <job-ref> --json   # {"jobRef":"job_...","status":"succeeded"}
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs explain <job-ref> --json   # what happened and what to do next
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs events  <job-ref> --json   # the timeline, newest first, --take <n> to bound it
```

- `-v q` keeps `dotnet run`'s own `Using launch settings from ...` line off stdout, so `--json` output pipes into `jq`; the launch profile, and with it the environment, still applies.
- `explain` first for anything stuck, waiting, or failed: one read of the status, lease, worker, newest
  steps, checkpoints, and latest reason, with a headline and the next actions.
- Without `--json` a verb answers in words. This is `jobs explain` on a job that waits for a signal, from
  `learn/000-fundamentals/021-jobs-cli`; a failed job's answer names the reason of its last attempt the same way:

  ```text
  job_01a1e8e75db8773582acdff65aaba15c  jobs-cli/review-document
  Suspended, waiting for signal "legal-approval".

  Last activity:
  - Last executed on worker wrk_01a1e8e75d937b5eb4f725fda6cf2418 (version 1.0.0).

  Next actions:
  - Raise signal "legal-approval".
  - Cancel the job.
  ```

- The verbs run beside the running app, on SQLite too: a read opens the file read-only, a control verb is one
  short write that waits its turn, and none of them starts a worker, migrates, or deploys (`migrate`, `deploy`
  and `debug` are the verbs that do).
- Exit codes: 0 found, applied, or already in state, 1 rejected or failed, 2 job not found, 64 usage error, 130 cancelled.
- On SQLite the reads open the file read-only: before `jobs migrate` has run they create nothing, print
  ``not provisioned; run `<app> jobs migrate` ``, and exit 1.
- `status`, `info`, `result`, `explain`, and `events` read. `cancel`, `pause`, `resume`, `restart`,
  `signal`, `clear-signal`, `debug` (runs the handler in this process), `deploy`, and `migrate` change things.
  All but `deploy` and `migrate` record `--actor <name>` as the actor on the job's event, and the operating
  system's user name without it.
- A `ready` job with a future due instant, or a `suspended` one, is healthy: it is waiting for its
  time or its signal, and `explain` names what it waits for. A caller's wait timeout stops only the
  wait; the job keeps running.
- The dashboard at `/acta` shows the same job, and `GET /acta/api/v1/jobs/{jobRef}` answers it as JSON; `GET /acta/api/v1/jobs/{jobRef}/detail` answers what the job page shows in one read, its explain included. No read but `/input`, `/result` and `/checkpoints/{checkpointKind}/{checkpointName}/value` carries a payload's body; the others state its format and size.

## Show jobs on your own screen

An app reads Acta through the services `UseActa` registers. Both are singletons, so inject them anywhere, a hosted
service or another singleton included.

- One job is `IJobs`. `GetAsync(jobRef)` answers the status, `NextRunAtUtc`, the lease, the parent, and the lane, or null when there is no such job; a laned job that is `Blocked` names the job that moves its lane on in `BlockedBehindJobRef`; `LeaseLapsed` is true for an executing job past its lease, whose worker stopped heartbeating. `Status.IsFinished` is true once the job landed `Succeeded`, `Failed`, or `Cancelled`. It also states the format and size of the input and of the result (`InputFormatId`, `InputByteLength`, `ResultFormatId`, `ResultByteLength`), so a screen knows a result exists, and how large it is, before it reads one. `GetStatusAsync`, `GetInputAsync`, `GetResultAsync<T>`, and `ExplainAsync` read one part. `var order = await jobs.GetInputAsync<ShipOrder>(jobRef, ct)` reads the input, as enqueued or last updated, as its type, and throws when no job matches. `ListStepsAsync(new ListJobStepsQuery(jobRef))` and `ListCheckpointsAsync(new ListJobCheckpointsQuery(jobRef))` list what the handler recorded, steps newest first and checkpoints by kind and name.
- Many jobs are `IActaOperations`. `acta.Ledger.ListJobsAsync(new ListJobsQuery(JobNamespace: "shipping", Status: JobStatusCode.Failed))` finds jobs, also by `JobName`, `Parent`, `CorrelationKey`, `Tags`, and `Lane`, and `Finished: false` lists the unfinished ones (`true` the finished). `acta.Ledger.ListEventsAsync(new ListEventsQuery(Job: job.JobRef))` reads a timeline, newest first, and `new ListEventsQuery(LineageRoot: root.JobRef)` reads a whole tree's in one query, children included. A timeline starts at the first attempt: the enqueue is the job's row (`CreatedAtUtc`), not an event. An event carries the job's `ExecutionNumber` as it stood when the event was written, so a `schedule.admitted` carries the number before the firing it starts; its details carry the firing id. A wait writes two events at one instant, `job.execution-yielded` (the execution's outcome) and `job.suspended` (the job's move), and a sleep writes `job.execution-yielded` and `job.slept`; a wait on a child reads `Child 'echo' pending.`, by the name the parent gave it when that attempt enqueued it (`Child job <id> pending.` when it was carried over in a variable), and the child's end resumes it with `job.signal-raised` reading `Child 'echo' succeeded.` (or `failed: ` and the child's message, or `cancelled.`, which is `cancelled: ` and the reason when the child's handler cancelled it with one); its details name the child, `{"child":"job_...","status":"succeeded"}`, and an operator's raise names its signal, `{"signal":"approved"}`. A raise that released the job writes `job.resumed` beside it with the reason `signal-released`; a raise the job was not parked on writes none. An execution reaches the timeline when it ends; the one running shows on `GetAsync` (`ExecutionNumber`, the lease). `Definitions`, `Schedules`, `Alerts`, and `Workers` sit beside `Ledger`.
- `await ctx.NoteAsync("Packed by Ana", ct)` writes a line of your own onto the job's timeline (`EventCode.JobNoteRecorded`), beside Acta's events. A note is written each time its line runs, so one before a wait or a sleep is written again when the job resumes: put it in a step, or after the last wait.
- A list answers a page: `Items`, `HasMore`, and `NextCursor`, which goes back in as the query's `Cursor`.
- A step shows `Name`, `Status`, `CreatedAtUtc`, and `ModifiedAtUtc`, and its result reads on its own: `await jobs.GetStepResultOrDefaultAsync<Receipt>(jobRef, "charge-card", ct)`, default until the step has succeeded with one. Any other value the screen needs goes in a variable, `await ctx.SetVariableAsync("stage", new Stage("packed", 3), ct)`, and the screen reads it with `await jobs.GetVariableOrDefaultAsync<Stage>(jobRef, "stage", ct)`, null until the handler has set it. A variable write is durable by itself and needs no step around it; a step is for work that must not run twice. `ctx.SetProgressAsync(value, ct)` keeps one "how far along" value, last write wins, as the checkpoint `sys.progress`, which Acta's dashboard lists with the job's checkpoints; a value your own screen reads goes in a variable, as above.
- The checkpoints also list what the job waits for: a `Signal` or a `Timer` with its `DueAtUtc`, and a `Child` per child. A variable's checkpoint has no `Status`. A checkpoint states its value's format and size (`ValueFormatId`, `ValueByteLength`) and not the value, which is its own read: `var read = await jobs.GetCheckpointValueAsync(jobRef, CheckpointKindCode.Signal, "approved", ct)`, null when the checkpoint holds none. `read.Value` is the payload as stored, so a raised signal's value reads with the serializer Acta wrote it with, `JsonJobPayloadSerializer.Default.Deserialize<Decision>(read.Value)` (with `JsonJobPayloadSerializer.WithResolver(...)` when the app registered a source-generated context with `UseJsonPayloads`).
- To label what a job is doing, read `jobs.ExplainAsync(jobRef)`: `Headline` says it in a sentence and `ActiveWait` names the wait it is parked on (`Kind`, `Name`, `DueAtUtc`), a child by the name its parent gave it. The status alone does not tell a sleep from a retry's backoff or a delayed start (each is `ready` with a future `NextRunAtUtc`), nor a wait for a person from a wait for a child (both `suspended`).
- A job between attempts reads `ready` with `FailureCount` above zero and its next attempt at `NextRunAtUtc`, and the step that threw reads `pending`. `FailureCount` is the retry budget's counter: the attempts that failed since the job last succeeded, a crash included, carried across waits and sleeps (a wait is not a success), and 0 again when the job succeeds; the events keep every failure. `ExecutionNumber` counts every claim of the job, each resume after a wait and each bounce off a full concurrency key included, so a parent that never failed can read execution 4: show `FailureCount` as the tries. A success says what it lost on the way: `ExplainAsync` reads `Succeeded after 1 lost lease and 2 failed attempts.`, counted from the job's events since its last restart. The exception's message is on the timeline, as the `Message` of each event whose `EventCode` is `EventCode.JobExecutionFailed`; an event also shows `CreatedAtUtc`, `DetailsText`, and `Actor`. A step's `FailureMessage` is set only for an at-most-once step that failed or was interrupted.
- Stored JSON has camelCase property names: `OrderId` is `orderId`.
- The text of every `*Code` value, a status, a kind, or an `EventCode`, is `.Code`: `job.Status.Code` is `suspended` and `EventCode.JobExecutionOrphaned.Code` is `job.execution-orphaned`, the text the CLI, the HTTP API, and SQL show, where `ToString()` gives the C# name `Suspended`. `JobStatusCodeExtensions.FromCode("suspended")` reads it back.
- Each read is its own snapshot, so two reads a moment apart can disagree while a job moves, and so is a read of your own table: an endpoint that reads both can show a record the handler wrote before the job reads `succeeded`. A sleeping job reads `ready` with a future `NextRunAtUtc`; a job waiting for a signal or a child reads `suspended`.
- `jobs.GetLineageMapAsync(jobRef)` answers one job with its `Ancestors` and its direct `Children`, each list capped and flagged (`ChildrenHasMore`). It is the neighbourhood of that job, not the whole tree: walk down by asking again for a child.
- `executing` means claimed, and the concurrency slot and the rate turn are taken after the claim. A count of `executing` jobs can therefore read above a `ConcurrencyLimit` for a moment; to show what is inside a gate, show the step the handler has reached.
- A page's script can call the same reads as JSON under `/acta/api/v1`, and a link to a job in Acta's dashboard is `/acta/#/jobs/{jobRef}`.
- The timings in force read from `IOptions<JobsOptions>`: `HeartbeatInterval` (45 s by default), and the two derived from it, `LeaseTtl` (four beats, 180 s) and `WorkerDeadAfter` (seven beats, 315 s).

## The HTTP API

`Acta.AspNetCore` serves Acta's operations over HTTP: `MapActaApi` maps the API alone, and `MapActa` from `Acta.Dashboard` maps it under `{pattern}/api/v1` beside the dashboard. Its contract is the OpenAPI document `docs/reference/openapi.json` in the repository. Generate a client from that document with standard OpenAPI tools; Acta ships no client package.

A payload travels in an envelope: `json` carries a JSON input as the value itself, and `base64` beside a `formatId` carries any other format. An enqueue, with controls enabled:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:5090/acta/api/v1/jobs -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jobNamespace":"shipping","jobName":"ship-order","input":{"json":{"orderId":1042}}}'   # 201, {"jobRef":"job_...","action":"inserted"}
```

## When you are unsure

Every pattern above exists as a compiled, runnable example under `learn/` in the repository:
numbered how-tos from fundamentals to chaos recovery, each a small project for one task, its program usually one
file named after the folder (`learn/200-durable-execution/215-map-wait-children/map-wait-children.cs`); the web hosts keep
theirs in `Program.cs`, and the testing how-tos hold test classes. The demo apps under
`demos/` are complete deployable applications built only from the published packages. The one
complete walk from enqueue to the first test, on the consumer packages, is `docs/first-job.md`; the
rest of the `docs/` tree is indexed by task in `docs/README.md`. Start at useacta.net.

The how-tos at useacta.net/learn teach one task each from those programs: the handler, the call that
starts it, the command that runs it, and the lines it must print. Every one is plain Markdown; the
list, by task, is useacta.net/learn/index.md.
